facts.text: Hope was a juvenile female blue whale. She stranded on a sandbar at the mouth of Wexford Harbour, Ireland, on the morning of 25 March 1891.
The 4.5-tonne skeleton was sold to the Natural History Museum for £250.
The skeleton hung in the museum's Mammal Hall from 1934.
The skeleton was moved to Hintze Hall and unveiled there in July 2017.
In Hintze Hall she replaced the cast of Dippy the Diplodocus, which stood there from 1979 until January 2017.
She was named Hope "as a symbol of humanity's power to shape a sustainable future".

unsourced_facts.text: The skeleton has 221 bones and is posed in a diving lunge.

title: Hope: the whale who came ashore

shots.narration: I am Hope. Long ago I was a young blue whale. On the morning of 25 March 1891, I stranded on a sandbar at the mouth of Wexford Harbour, in Ireland.
shots.action: First the huge blue whale skeleton hanging in a museum hall softly fills out into a living blue whale. Then she swims through open ocean and does one slow roll. Then, at dawn, she drifts into shallow water and comes to rest on a pale sandbar as small waves wash around her.

shots.narration: My skeleton was sold to the museum for 250 pounds. In July 2017 I was unveiled here in Hintze Hall. They named me Hope: a symbol of humanity's power to shape a sustainable future.
shots.action: First the whale floats past wooden crates in a storeroom as her body turns softly translucent, a glowing skeleton showing inside. Then she sweeps down into a grand museum hall in one long glide as visitors look up, turns to face the viewer and comes gently closer.
